subject_line: After the Aiken Taylor: Erase Genesis and the translator's ear
email_body:
Dear Rebecca,

Congratulations on the 2025 Aiken Taylor Award for Modern American Poetry. Reading about it, I was struck by how many lives your work holds at once: ten years as poetry editor of the Oxford American, translations of Claudia Prado and Amal al-Jubouri, and now Erase Genesis on the way.

For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask how translating other poets has changed the way you hear your own lines, and what the title Erase Genesis is pushing against.

The Author Ledger is an independent project featuring short Author Spotlights. The portrait is developed through a few written questions, which you can answer at your own pace, and the full text is shared with you for review before publication.

Would you be open to taking part?

Best regards,
The Author Ledger

subject_line: Grief and rebirth in One Wild Word Away
email_body:
Dear Geffrey,

One Wild Word Away holds illness, family and loss alongside rebirth, and the Southern Review of Books described poems haunted by grief that still lean toward hope. After Revising the Storm and Night Angler, it reads like a third turn in a long conversation about fathers, sons and repair.

I'd be curious to ask how you decide when a poem has earned its hope rather than reaching for it, and how teaching in the Arkansas creative writing and translation program shapes that sense.

book_title: On Earth As It Is Beneath (translation of Ana Paula Maia)
subject_line: Carrying Ana Paula Maia's On Earth As It Is Beneath into English
email_body:
Dear Padma,

Seeing your translation of Ana Paula Maia's On Earth As It Is Beneath move from the 2026 International Booker long list to the shortlist, I was glad that a Brazilian novella of this kind found such a wide audience, and that the prize divides its recognition equally between author and translator.

For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask what was hardest to carry from Maia's Portuguese into English, and how translating sits beside your own fiction and your teaching in Arkansas.

email_body:

In your Milkweed conversation about Horses, you said the new book feels more like a debut than your first one did, since Eyes Bottle Dark with a Mouthful of Flowers was written entirely during your MFA. Coming after a National Poetry Series selection and a Whiting Award, that surprised me.

For a Spotlight, I'd ask what changed in how you wrote Horses, and how serving as Navajo Nation Poet Laureate has shaped the work.

subject_line: Milton Muleborn and the 1988 detention center
email_body:
Dear Brandon,

The Devil Is a Southpaw puts us in the hands of Milton Muleborn, an unreliable narrator in an Oklahoma juvenile detention facility in 1988, and I was drawn to how you describe its themes: the trauma of incarceration, mental health, forgiveness, and the envy of artists.

For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask where the envy between artists entered the book, and how writing a sixth novel differs from writing Where the Dead Sit Talking.

For a Spotlight, I'd ask how the beasts of the title came to carry so much of the collection, and how prose in the memoir let you say things a poem would not.

subject_line: The Camera Poems in An Arm Fixed to a Wing
email_body:
Dear Olivia,

In the Southern Miss Q&A about An Arm Fixed to a Wing, you described poetry as holding "all large and small things at once," and the central Camera Poems sequence seems to test that, moving between isolation, hope and self-awareness, with motherhood running through several pieces.

For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask why the camera became the frame for that sequence, and how moving between a novel, stories and poems has changed what you ask of each form.

subject_line: The invasive wasps of Wasp Box
email_body:
Dear Jason,

Wasp Box starts from a striking premise: a soldier comes home to a small New York town and brings an invasive species of deadly wasps with him, and a whole community tips into crisis. Alongside the stories in Rabbit Punches and Neighbors of Nothing, it shows how one strange intrusion can unsettle ordinary lives.

For a Spotlight, I'd ask where that image of the wasps came from, and what you are working on now while teaching fiction at Coastal Carolina.

subject_line: Candles, hymns and Black Creek in Living Things
email_body:
Dear Landon,

Living Things is set in Black Creek, a fictional rural town modelled on Darlington, South Carolina, where tragedy is met with candles, hymns and the urge to leave. I was curious that a writer from Bangs, Texas, chose to build a novel so closely on a Pee Dee town near where you teach.

For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask how Darlington became Black Creek on the page, and what has kept you writing about the South since the book's launch in Florence.

subject_line: Two stepsisters meeting in The Tender Grave
email_body:
Dear Sheri,

The Tender Grave came nine years after your previous novel, and it takes on a hate crime, the poisons a dysfunctional family releases, and the first meeting of two stepsisters from very different worlds. Its home at Bywater Books, a feminist and lesbian press, struck me as a deliberate choice.

For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask what brought you back to the novel after that long gap, and how coordinating creative writing at Wofford feeds your own work now.

email_body:

Dream City is described as an unconventional portrait and fictional history of Las Vegas in the boom years before the Great Recession, which feels like a natural arc from Leaving the Land, a novel also about what an economy does to a place and its people.

For a Spotlight, I'd ask how long you had been gathering Las Vegas before it became a novel, and whether the craft essays in Geometries of Fiction grew out of writing it.

subject_line: Angela's prison narrative in The Last Language
email_body:
Dear Jennifer,

In The Last Language, Angela writes from prison about a young nonverbal man who seems to speak only through her, by way of facilitated communication, and the Chicago Review of Books noted how the reader grows less sure whether the two are conversing at all.

For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask how you kept that ambiguity open without tipping it, and what drew you to a narrator so invested in language.

email_body:
Dear Cecily,

The Seeds, your third collection from Alice James Books, brings motherhood together with Persephone and Demeter, and the Mom Egg Review piece followed how a single tree and the Texas landscape thread through the book. That pairing of an old mother-daughter myth with close ecological attention feels very particular to you.

For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask how the myth entered poems so rooted in Central Texas, and what the title's seeds meant to you as the book took shape.

subject_line: Eight weeks to write The World That the Shooter Left Us
email_body:
Dear Cyrus,

You've said The World That the Shooter Left Us poured through you in the space of eight weeks, after the Stand Your Ground killing of a close friend's father. The Poetry Foundation reviewer felt its strongest poems carry their civic anger through the intimacy of personal relationships.

For a Spotlight, I'd ask what it was like to write at that speed, and how your year as Texas Poet Laureate shaped the way you think about poems speaking to the public.

email_body:
Dear Kerry,

Nine Persimmons, your new collection from Backwaters Press, is described as finding the divinity the ordinary gathers on its own, through details like persimmon seeds and a grandmother's gospel singing. It arrives a good while after Bangalore, your Lannan Literary Selection from Copper Canyon.

For a Spotlight, I'd like to ask why the persimmon became the book's governing image, and how the years between the two collections changed what you wanted from a poem, including your work running the MFA at Georgia College.
